source_evidence.location: PDF page 1; printed page 5; Section 1.1 "Basic quantities associated with random variables", first displayed formula
source_evidence.anchor: "In a basic course in probability theory, we learned about the two most important quantities associated with a random variable X, namely the expectation1 (also called mean), and variance. They will be denoted in this book by2  E X   and   Var(X) = E(X − E X)2 ."
source_evidence.observation: This is the sole defining/notational statement for the row. It fixes (a) the notation `E X` for the expectation of a random variable X, also called the mean, and (b) the notation and defining formula `Var(X) = E(X − E X)^2` for the variance. The variance is given by an explicit formula in terms of expectation; the expectation itself is not given a formula in the body text, only in footnote 1. The binder is a single random variable X; no further hypotheses (integrability, boundedness, non-negativity, discreteness, independence) are attached in the displayed line.

source_evidence.location: PDF page 1; printed page 5; footnote 1 (attached to the word "expectation" in Section 1.1)
source_evidence.anchor: "If you studied measure theory, you will recall that the expectation E X of a random variable X on a probability space (Ω, Σ, P) is, by definition, the Lebesgue integral of the function X : Ω → R. This makes all theorems on Lebesgue integration applicable in probability theory, for expectations of random variables."
source_evidence.observation: Footnote 1 is the definitional content of `E X`: expectation IS, by definition, the Lebesgue integral of X with respect to the probability measure P. It also fixes the ambient objects: a probability space (Ω, Σ, P) — sample space, σ-algebra, probability measure — and a real-valued random variable X : Ω → R (codomain R, not the extended reals, not C, not a vector space). The stated purpose of the footnote is transfer of Lebesgue-integration theorems to expectations.

source_evidence.location: PDF page 1; printed page 5; footnote 2 (attached to "denoted in this book by")
source_evidence.anchor: "Throughout this book, we drop the brackets in the notation E[f (X)] and simply write E f (X) instead. Thus, nonlinear functions bind before expectation."
source_evidence.observation: Book-wide parsing convention that disambiguates the variance display: `E(X − E X)^2` means `E[(X − E X)^2]`, i.e. the squaring is applied pointwise to the centered variable X − E X and the expectation is taken of the result. It does NOT mean `(E(X − E X))^2` (which would be 0). The same convention governs `E X^p`, `E |X|^p`, `E e^{tX}` later on the page.

Inherited standing hypothesis (chapter-level): P is a probability measure, so P(Ω) = 1; this is what makes the Lebesgue integral of X against P the 'expectation'/'mean' rather than a general integral.
Inherited standing hypothesis (footnote 1): X is real-valued (codomain R). The passage does not treat extended-real-valued, complex, or vector-valued random variables here.

Module definability policy (analyst-configured interpretation, NOT printed in the first edition): the displayed real expression `E X` is read on its finite-integral domain, i.e. under `Integrable X` (X measurable with E|X| < ∞), and `Var(X) = E(X − E X)^2` is read under square-integrability `MemLp X 2` (which supplies both that (X − E X)^2 has finite integral and, since P is finite, that E X itself is defined). Per the configured module convention these premises are part of the source contract because they are what make the displayed real-valued expressions meaningful; they are not optional proof conveniences.

Note on the printed text's own silence: because the source states no exceptional-value convention, the above premises are an interpretation layered onto the passage, not a transcription of it. See ambiguities.
conclusions: Definition/notation (expectation): for a random variable X on (Ω, Σ, P), the symbol `E X` denotes the expectation of X, also called the mean — literally "the expectation1 (also called mean)" … "denoted in this book by2 E X".

Definition (expectation, footnote 1, the semantic content): `E X` is, BY DEFINITION, the Lebesgue integral of the function X : Ω → R with respect to P. In integral notation E X = ∫_Ω X dP. The footnote's stated consequence: "This makes all theorems on Lebesgue integration applicable in probability theory, for expectations of random variables."

Definition (variance): `Var(X) = E(X − E X)^2`, i.e. by footnote 2's binding convention, Var(X) = E[(X − E X)^2] — the expectation of the square of the centered random variable X − E X. The centering constant subtracted is exactly E X (the variable's own mean), and the square is applied pointwise on Ω before the outer expectation.

Structural consequence made explicit two paragraphs later (printed page 6): Var(X) = ∥X − E X∥_{L2}^2, and sqrt(Var(X)) = ∥X − E X∥_{L2} = σ(X) is the standard deviation. This confirms Var(X) ≥ 0 under the L2 reading, though non-negativity is not asserted as a separate claim at the definition site.

This row is definitional/notational: there is no theorem, no inequality, no bound, and no proof obligation at this location. The 'result' to be preserved is exactly the pair of definitions plus the Lebesgue-integral identification and the bracket-dropping parse.
definitions_and_conventions: Expectation (a.k.a. mean), notation `E X`, defined as the Lebesgue integral ∫_Ω X dP of X : Ω → R over the probability space (Ω, Σ, P) (footnote 1, verbatim: "is, by definition, the Lebesgue integral of the function X : Ω → R").
Variance, notation `Var(X)`, defined as `E(X − E X)^2` (Section 1.1 display).

Bracket-dropping convention (footnote 2, verbatim): "Throughout this book, we drop the brackets in the notation E[f (X)] and simply write E f (X) instead. Thus, nonlinear functions bind before expectation." Hence `E(X − E X)^2` = `E[(X − E X)^2]`, NOT `(E(X − E X))^2`. The inner `E X` in `X − E X` is itself a real constant, so the centered object X − E X is again a random variable on Ω.
Probability space notation `(Ω, Σ, P)` fixed by footnote 1 and reused on printed page 6 ("for fixed p and a given probability space (Ω, Σ, P)").

Random variable = a (measurable) function X : Ω → R; the source does not restate the measurability requirement at this point, treating it as recalled from an introductory course ("The reader should already be familiar with most of this material").

Nearby but out-of-scope for this row (same section, do not conflate): moment generating function M_X(t) = E e^{tX}; p-th moment E X^p and p-th absolute moment E |X|^p for p > 0; Lp norm ∥X∥_{Lp} = (E |X|^p)^{1/p} for p ∈ (0, ∞); ∥X∥_{L∞} = ess sup |X|; L2 inner product ⟨X, Y⟩_{L2} = E XY; standard deviation σ(X); covariance cov(X, Y).

Module definability convention applied by this audit (analyst-configured, printed source is silent): each ordinary real-valued `E X` is read on its finite-integral domain — `Integrable X` for an expectation, `MemLp X 2` (square-integrability) for a variance.
implicit_context: Chapter 1 is declared recall material: "In this chapter we recall some basic concepts and results of probability theory. The reader should already be familiar with most of this material, which is routinely taught in introductory probability courses." Standard measure-theoretic background is therefore assumed rather than developed.
Measurability of X with respect to Σ is inherited from the phrase 'random variable' and from the appeal to Lebesgue integration; it is nowhere spelled out in the passage.

P(Ω) = 1 (probability measure) is inherited from the notation (Ω, Σ, P) and the word 'probability space'. Consequence used implicitly later: finiteness of P makes L2 ⊆ L1 (spelled out only later, at inequality (1.3) on printed page 6, ∥X∥_{Lp} ≤ ∥X∥_{Lq} for 0 ≤ p ≤ q ≤ ∞).

Linearity/monotonicity/Fubini-Tonelli and the rest of Lebesgue integration are imported wholesale by footnote 1's stated purpose; the first actual use of that import is Lemma 1.2.1's proof on printed page 7.

The natural domain of Var(X) is L2 = L2(Ω, Σ, P) = {X : ∥X∥_{L2} < ∞}, defined on printed page 6 — but the definition of Var(X) on printed page 5 textually PRECEDES that L2 definition and is stated without reference to it.

Analyst inference (flagged as such, not printed): under the module's square-integrability reading, Var(X) is a finite non-negative real and the alternative form Var(X) = E X^2 − (E X)^2 follows; the source never writes that alternative form in this passage.

details: X: the single random variable under discussion; role = the object whose expectation and variance are being defined. Real-valued function on Ω.
E: an operator (not a number) mapping a random variable to a real number, realized as Lebesgue integration against P.
E X: a deterministic real number (a constant), used in two roles — as the defined quantity itself, and as the centering constant inside the variance formula.
X − E X: the centered random variable, again a function on Ω; it is the argument of the outer expectation in the variance definition (and the L2 vector whose norm squared is the variance).
Var(X): a deterministic real number attached to X.
(Ω, Σ, P): ambient parameter triple, fixed throughout, never varied within the row.

The only numeric constant in the row is the exponent 2 in `E(X − E X)^2`. It is a literal, not a parameter; the p-indexed generalizations (p-th moment, Lp norm) are separate definitions in the same section and are not this row.
No index sets, no sample size n, no dimension, no absolute constants C or c appear anywhere in this row.
No hidden multiplicative or additive constants: the variance formula is an exact identity of definition, not an up-to-constant statement.

The definitions are stated schematically for 'a random variable X', which in context means: for every probability space (Ω, Σ, P) and every real random variable X on it, the symbols E X and Var(X) have the stated meaning.
The probability space is quantified outermost and the random variable inside it (X depends on Ω); there is no quantifier alternation subtlety and no uniformity claim of any kind.
Nothing in this row is an implication with a nontrivial antecedent; both items are definitional equalities/notational stipulations.

semantic_facets.topic: Exceptional cases and domain of definition
details: The source states no exceptional-value convention: it does not say what E X is when the Lebesgue integral fails to exist (e.g. E X^+ = E X^− = ∞), nor when it is infinite for signed X.

The only place in the surrounding text where an infinite expectation is admitted is Lemma 1.2.1 (printed page 7), explicitly for a NON-NEGATIVE random variable, with the qualifier "The two sides of this identity are either finite or infinite simultaneously". This does not generalize to arbitrary real X within the audited passage.
Correspondingly the source never says whether Var(X) may be +∞ or undefined for X ∉ L2.

Module definability policy resolves both by restriction of domain rather than by junk values: `Integrable X` for E X, `MemLp X 2` for Var(X). Under this policy both quantities are finite reals wherever they are asserted.
Degenerate cases not discussed by the source: constant X (Var = 0), and whether Var(X) = 0 forces X constant a.s. — no such converse is claimed here.

semantic_facets.topic: Notation-parsing hazards (must be preserved in any formalization)
details: `E(X − E X)^2` must be parsed as E[(X − E X)^2]. Footnote 2 makes this a book-wide rule: 'nonlinear functions bind before expectation'. Mis-parsing as (E(X − E X))^2 collapses the definition to 0.
The inner `E X` is the mean of the SAME variable X, not an independent copy and not a second variable; the centering is self-centering.
The square is applied pointwise on Ω, i.e. ω ↦ (X(ω) − E X)^2; it is not |X − E X|^2 written differently in any meaningful sense here, since X is real-valued (for real X the two coincide).
`E X` in the first display carries no brackets and no measure subscript; the measure is always P from the ambient probability space.

semantic_facets.topic: What is NOT claimed at this location

No claim about existence/uniqueness of E X, no claim about a.s.-equal variables having equal expectation, no claim about translation/scaling behaviour of Var.
No independence, no distributional assumption, no sequence or limit content.
Printed page 6, display (1.1) and following line: L2 inner product/norm and ∥X − E X∥_{L2} = sqrt(Var(X)) = σ(X) — corroborates the intended L2 reading of the variance.
Printed page 6, definition of Lp = Lp(Ω, Σ, P) = {X : ∥X∥_{Lp} < ∞} — the source's own finite-norm restriction idiom, the closest printed analogue of the module's integrability premises.
Printed page 6, inequality (1.3) ∥X∥_{Lp} ≤ ∥X∥_{Lq} for 0 ≤ p ≤ q ≤ ∞ — the source's justification that L2 membership implies L1 membership on a probability space.
Printed page 6, display (1.2) covariance — the two-variable analogue whose diagonal is the variance.
Printed page 7, Lemma 1.2.1 — the only nearby place where an infinite expectation is countenanced, and only for non-negative X.

undebatable_constraints: `E X` must denote the expectation (mean) of a real-valued random variable X on a probability space (Ω, Σ, P), realized as the Lebesgue integral of X : Ω → R with respect to P — footnote 1: "is, by definition, the Lebesgue integral of the function X : Ω → R". Any formalization that uses a non-integral notion of expectation (e.g. a finite/discrete sum only, or a Riemann/Stieltjes-only formulation) breaks the contract.
The underlying measure must be a PROBABILITY measure (P(Ω) = 1), per "a probability space (Ω, Σ, P)". A general measure space is not faithful.
X must be real-valued (codomain R as printed in footnote 1). Not extended-real, not complex, not vector-valued at this location.

`Var(X)` must be defined as `E(X − E X)^2`, parsed via footnote 2 as `E[(X − E X)^2]`: the expectation of the pointwise square of the self-centered variable. The alternative parse (E(X − E X))^2 is wrong and would be identically zero.
The centering constant inside the variance must be `E X` for the same X — not an arbitrary constant, not a median, not zero.
The exponent in the variance is exactly 2 (a literal), not a general p.

Both items of the row must be preserved together: the expectation notation/definition (with its footnote-1 Lebesgue-integral identification) AND the variance definition. Dropping either half, or dropping the Lebesgue-integral identification, under-covers the row.

The row is definitional/notational. It asserts no inequality, no bound, no non-negativity, and no algebraic identity such as Var(X) = E X^2 − (E X)^2; a formalization must not present such extras as if they were the source's claim at this location.

ambiguities.issue: The first-edition source states no integrability hypothesis and no exceptional-value convention for `E X` when the Lebesgue integral of X does not exist or is infinite. It is silent on the domain of definition of the expectation operator for arbitrary real random variables.
ambiguities.evidence: Printed page 5, Section 1.1: "we learned about the two most important quantities associated with a random variable X, namely the expectation1 (also called mean), and variance. They will be denoted in this book by2 E X and Var(X) = E(X − E X)2." Footnote 1: "the expectation E X of a random variable X on a probability space (Ω, Σ, P) is, by definition, the Lebesgue integral of the function X : Ω → R." No qualifier such as 'assume E|X| < ∞' or 'X ∈ L1' appears anywhere in Sections 1.1–1.2. The only admission of an infinite expectation is scoped to non-negative X in Lemma 1.2.1 (printed page 7): "Let X be a non-negative random variable. … The two sides of this identity are either finite or infinite simultaneously."
ambiguities.impact: Per this module's authoritative interpretation policy, the ordinary real-valued `E X` is read on its finite-integral domain, i.e. under the premise `Integrable X`. That premise is treated as part of the configured source contract because it is what makes the displayed real expression meaningful — not as a proof convenience — but a judge must be aware it is a module-level interpretation supplied by policy, not literal printed wording. A formalization that instead assigns a junk/zero value to a non-integrable expectation, or that quantifies over all measurable X with no premise, is resolving the source's silence differently and should be flagged rather than silently accepted.

ambiguities.issue: Likewise, no square-integrability hypothesis is printed for the variance, and the L2 space that would supply it is defined only AFTER the variance definition.

contract_plain_english: Vershynin, HDP first edition, Chapter 1 ("Preliminaries on random variables"), Section 1.1 ("Basic quantities associated with random variables"), printed page 5, introduces — as recalled background, not as a theorem — the two basic quantities attached to a random variable X: its expectation (also called the mean), written E X, and its variance, written and defined by the display Var(X) = E(X − E X)^2. Footnote 1 supplies the actual meaning of the expectation: for a random variable X on a probability space (Ω, Σ, P), E X is by definition the Lebesgue integral of the function X : Ω → R against P, the stated point being that all theorems of Lebesgue integration then apply to expectations. Footnote 2 supplies the parsing rule used throughout the book: brackets are dropped from E[f(X)], so nonlinear functions bind before expectation; hence the variance display means E[(X − E X)^2] — the expectation of the pointwise square of the self-centered variable X − E X — and emphatically not (E(X − E X))^2, which would be zero. The centering constant is the mean of the same X, and the exponent 2 is a literal, not a parameter. Two paragraphs later (printed page 6) the book confirms this reading by writing ∥X − E X∥_{L2} = sqrt(Var(X)) = σ(X), placing the variance's natural home in L2(Ω, Σ, P) = {X : ∥X∥_{L2} < ∞}. The passage attaches no hypotheses of its own — no integrability, boundedness, non-negativity, or distributional assumption — and states no convention for what E X should be when the Lebesgue integral fails to exist; the only nearby admission of an infinite expectation is Lemma 1.2.1 on printed page 7, restricted to non-negative X. Because the first edition is silent there, this book module fixes the reading by policy: each ordinary real-valued E X is taken on its finite-integral domain, so an expectation carries the premise Integrable X and a variance carries square-integrability MemLp X 2 (which on a probability space also makes the inner E X well-defined). Those premises are part of the configured contract — they are what make the displayed real expressions meaningful — but they are a module interpretation, not printed wording, and are recorded as such. Nothing else is asserted at this location: no non-negativity, no linearity, no identity Var(X) = E X^2 − (E X)^2, no inequality. A faithful formalization must preserve both halves of the row together — the Lebesgue-integral expectation E X and the centered-second-moment variance Var(X) = E[(X − E X)^2] — over a real-valued random variable on a probability space, and must remain definitional in character.
